$comment: Course catalogue for the CS Virtual Lab. Courses are identified by slug and shown by name; institutional codes are kept only as reference metadata. Generated by build-courses.mjs from htu-curriculum-2022.json, the extended list and programmes.json. Do not edit by hand.

programmes.title: Computer Science
programmes.description: The science of computation: programming, algorithms, theory, systems and their applications. Every practical, from wiring logic gates to training models, runs in the browser.
outcomes: Design, implement and analyse algorithms and data structures.
Build software across the stack, from low-level code to web and mobile applications.
Explain how computers, operating systems and networks work and configure them.
Apply mathematics, data and artificial intelligence to real problems responsibly.

programmes.title: Computer Engineering
programmes.description: Where hardware meets software: circuits, digital systems, processors, embedded devices and the signals they handle. Students build and test circuits, microcontroller programs and control loops on simulated benches.
outcomes: Analyse analogue and digital circuits and design combinational and sequential logic.
Program microcontrollers and processors at the register and assembly level.
Process signals and design filters and feedback controllers.
Design embedded and connected systems that work within power and cost limits.

programmes.title: Software Engineering
programmes.description: Building software that works, lasts and can be trusted: requirements, design, testing, delivery and teamwork. Students practise on real codebases, pipelines and review exercises.
outcomes: Elicit and specify requirements with users and stakeholders.
Design maintainable systems using patterns and sound architecture.
Test, review and deliver software through automated pipelines.
Plan and run software projects in teams, securely and ethically.

programmes.title: Data Analytics
programmes.description: Turning raw data into decisions: cleaning, querying, analysing and presenting data for organisations. Students work with spreadsheets, SQL, code and dashboards on realistic local datasets.
outcomes: Collect, clean and prepare data from spreadsheets, databases and files.
Query and summarise data with SQL and code.
Apply statistical methods to answer business and public questions.
Communicate findings with clear charts, dashboards and reports.

programmes.title: Data Science
programmes.description: The mathematics, statistics and computing behind learning from data at scale. Students build models end to end, from collection and cleaning to evaluation and communication.
outcomes: Use linear algebra, calculus and probability to reason about data and models.
Prepare, explore and visualise large and messy datasets.
Build, evaluate and explain statistical and machine learning models.
Process data at scale and handle it lawfully and ethically.

programmes.title: Information Systems
programmes.description: How organisations use information technology to work, decide and serve people. Students model business processes, design databases and evaluate systems through case scenarios.
outcomes: Analyse business processes and the information they need.
Design and manage databases and enterprise systems.
Plan, govern and evaluate information technology investments.
Protect information and respect privacy and the law.

programmes.title: Machine Learning
programmes.description: Building systems that learn from data, from the mathematics to deployment. Students implement algorithms from scratch, then train, evaluate and ship models within modest compute budgets.
outcomes: Derive and implement core learning algorithms using linear algebra, calculus and probability.
Train and tune deep networks for text, images and sequences.
Evaluate models rigorously and diagnose failure.
Deploy, monitor and govern models responsibly.

programmes.title: Cloud Computing
programmes.description: Running software on shared, programmable infrastructure: networks, servers, containers and automation. Students provision, secure and operate services in simulated cloud consoles and terminals.
outcomes: Configure networks, servers and operating systems.
Package and run applications with containers and orchestrators.
Automate infrastructure and delivery with code and pipelines.
Secure, monitor and keep cloud services reliable and affordable.

programmes.title: Bioinformatics
programmes.description: Computing applied to biology: sequences, genomes, proteins and evolution. Students align sequences, assemble genomes and build trees with browser-based tools and real public data.
outcomes: Explain the molecular biology behind biological data.
Implement and apply sequence alignment and search algorithms.
Analyse sequencing data from reads to variants and expression.
Use statistics and machine learning on biological data, including for disease surveillance.

programmes.title: Health Informatics
programmes.description: Information systems and data for better health care and public health. Students design patient records, exchange data with health standards and analyse outbreaks in case-based simulations.
outcomes: Describe how health systems collect and use information.
Design and evaluate health information systems and electronic records.
Exchange health data using international standards.
Analyse health data while protecting patient privacy.

programmes.title: Robotics
programmes.description: Machines that sense, decide and act: electronics, mechanics, control and intelligence together. Students program simulated robots, tune controllers and plan paths before touching hardware.
outcomes: Model robot motion with kinematics and dynamics.
Interface sensors and actuators through embedded programs.
Design controllers and real-time software for robots.
Give robots perception, localisation and planning.

programmes.title: Cybersecurity
programmes.description: Protecting systems, networks and data, and responding when attacks happen. Students attack and defend isolated virtual machines and networks safely inside the browser.
outcomes: Secure operating systems, networks and applications.
Find and responsibly report vulnerabilities through testing.
Detect, investigate and respond to incidents.
Apply cryptography and work within the law and ethics.

programmes.title: Artificial Intelligence
programmes.description: Building systems that reason, learn, perceive and act, and doing so responsibly. Students implement search, logic and learning algorithms and test them in simulated environments.
outcomes: Apply search, logic and probabilistic reasoning to problems.
Build learning systems for language, vision and decision making.
Evaluate AI systems for accuracy, fairness and safety.
Design AI that suits local languages, data and constraints.

programmes.title: Information Technology
programmes.description: Keeping the technology of organisations running: hardware, networks, servers, users and services. Students troubleshoot, configure and support systems in simulated workplaces.
outcomes: Install, troubleshoot and maintain hardware and software.
Set up and run networks and servers.
Support users and manage IT services well.
Keep systems secure, backed up and compliant.

programmes.title: Networking and Telecommunications
programmes.description: The networks that connect people: data links, the internet, mobile and wireless systems. Students design, configure and troubleshoot networks and radio links in simulators.
outcomes: Explain how signals carry data over wired, wireless and optical media.
Design, address and route networks and secure them.
Describe and plan mobile and cellular networks.
Use programmable and virtualised networks.

programmes.title: Game Development
programmes.description: Designing and programming games, including games that teach. Students prototype mechanics, write engine code and simulate physics that runs on everyday phones.
outcomes: Design game mechanics, levels and player experiences.
Program games with graphics, input, audio and physics.
Use mathematics for movement, collisions and cameras.
Test games with players and ship them to phones and the web.

programmes.title: Financial Technology
programmes.description: Technology for money: payments, mobile money, credit, ledgers and the rules around them. Students build payment flows, model risk and work through compliance cases drawn from African markets.
outcomes: Explain how payment systems and mobile money work.
Build secure financial applications and data pipelines.
Model interest, risk and credit with mathematics and data.
Work within financial regulation and protect customers.

courses.title: Basic Electronics
topics: Semiconductor physics: energy bands, carriers, n and p material
Diodes: bias, V-I curve, Zener, rectifiers, filters, regulated supplies, clippers, clampers, multipliers, datasheets
BJT: operation, CE/CB/CC, load line, biasing, thermal stability, switching
Digital circuits: gates, diode gates, logic families RTL/DTL/TTL/CMOS
RLC circuits series and parallel
Signals: continuous/discrete, even/odd, periodic, power/energy
courses.description: From the physics of silicon to working amplifier and logic circuits, with every circuit built, measured and simulated rather than only drawn. Taught to the depth of a first-year engineering circuits course, with every circuit simulated and measured.
modelledOn: Sedra and Smith, Microelectronic Circuits
Agarwal and Lang, Foundations of Analog and Digital Electronic Circuits
Boylestad and Nashelsky, Electronic Devices and Circuit Theory
outcomes: Analyse DC and AC circuits with Kirchhoff's laws, node and mesh analysis, Thevenin and Norton equivalents.
Explain how carriers move in doped silicon and derive the diode and transistor V-I behaviour from it.
Design rectifiers, regulators, clippers and clampers and predict their waveforms.
Bias a BJT amplifier for stable operation and compute its gain, input and output resistance.
Analyse RLC circuits in the time and frequency domains and read resonance and bandwidth from a plot.
Classify signals and relate the continuous and discrete views of them to later signal processing courses.

syllabus.title: Circuit fundamentals and lab practice
topics: Charge, current, voltage, power and energy; passive sign convention
Resistors, Ohm's law, series and parallel combinations, voltage and current dividers
Kirchhoff's current and voltage laws; node-voltage and mesh-current analysis
Superposition, Thevenin and Norton equivalents, maximum power transfer
Using a breadboard, multimeter, oscilloscope and bench supply; reading a datasheet
Dependent sources and the ideal operational amplifier as a circuit element

syllabus.title: Semiconductor physics
topics: Energy bands in conductors, insulators and semiconductors; band gap of silicon and germanium
Intrinsic carriers, electrons and holes; temperature dependence
Doping: donors and acceptors, n-type and p-type material, majority and minority carriers
Drift and diffusion currents; mobility and conductivity
The p-n junction at equilibrium: depletion region, built-in potential

syllabus.title: Diodes and diode circuits
topics: Forward and reverse bias; the diode equation and the V-I curve; ideal, constant-drop and piecewise models
Zener breakdown and avalanche; Zener regulators and line/load regulation
Half-wave, full-wave centre-tap and bridge rectifiers; ripple and capacitor filters
Regulated DC supplies: transformer, rectifier, filter, regulator (78xx and LM317)
Clippers, clampers and voltage multipliers; LED and photodiode circuits
Reading a diode datasheet: PIV, forward drop, maximum current, recovery time

syllabus.title: Bipolar junction transistors
topics: NPN and PNP structure and operation; active, saturation and cut-off regions; alpha and beta
Common-emitter, common-base and common-collector configurations and their characteristics
DC load line and Q-point; fixed, emitter and voltage-divider biasing; bias stability and thermal runaway
Small-signal model (hybrid-pi) and the gain, input and output resistance of a CE amplifier
The transistor as a switch: driving an LED, a relay and a small DC motor
Introduction to MOSFETs: enhancement-mode NMOS and PMOS, threshold voltage, regions of operation

syllabus.title: Operational amplifiers
topics: Ideal op-amp rules; inverting, non-inverting, summing and difference amplifiers
Integrators, differentiators and active filters
Comparators, Schmitt triggers and simple oscillators
Real op-amp limits: offset, slew rate, gain-bandwidth product

syllabus.title: Digital circuits and logic families
topics: Voltage levels, noise margins and the transfer characteristic of an inverter
Diode logic AND and OR gates and why they cannot be cascaded
RTL, DTL and TTL gate construction; totem-pole output; fan-out and propagation delay
CMOS inverter, NAND and NOR; static and dynamic power
Interfacing logic families and level shifting; open-collector and tri-state outputs

syllabus.title: Capacitors, inductors and RLC circuits
topics: Capacitor and inductor V-I relations; energy storage; RC and RL transients and time constants
Sinusoidal steady state: phasors, impedance and admittance
Series and parallel RLC circuits: resonance frequency, quality factor, bandwidth
Frequency response and Bode plots; low-pass, high-pass and band-pass filters
Second-order transients: underdamped, critically damped and overdamped responses

syllabus.title: Signals
topics: Continuous-time and discrete-time signals; sampling as the bridge between them
Even and odd decomposition; periodic and aperiodic signals
Energy and power signals; RMS value of common waveforms
Standard signals: impulse, step, ramp, exponential and sinusoid
Reading a signal on an oscilloscope: amplitude, period, frequency, phase, DC offset

courses.title: Discrete Mathematics
topics: Set theory and binary operations
Number systems
Functions and relations
Sequence and series
Induction and recursion
Graph theory
Logic
Boolean algebra
courses.description: The mathematics that computer science is written in: logic, proof, sets, relations, counting, number theory and graphs, taught by proving and computing rather than memorising. Taught to the depth of the standard mathematics-for-computer-science course, with every proof technique practised on real problems.
modelledOn: Rosen, Discrete Mathematics and Its Applications
Lehman, Leighton and Meyer, Mathematics for Computer Science
Epp, Discrete Mathematics with Applications
outcomes: Translate English statements into propositional and predicate logic and check validity with truth tables and inference rules.
Write correct proofs by direct argument, contrapositive, contradiction, cases and induction, including strong and structural induction.
Work fluently with sets, functions and relations, and prove properties such as injectivity, equivalence and partial order.
Count arrangements with permutations, combinations, the pigeonhole principle and inclusion-exclusion, and solve recurrences.
Apply modular arithmetic, GCD and the Chinese remainder theorem, including to RSA.
Model problems as graphs and reason about paths, trees, colourings and planarity.

syllabus.title: Propositional and predicate logic
topics: Propositions, connectives, truth tables, tautologies and contradictions
Logical equivalence, De Morgan's laws, conditional and biconditional, converse and contrapositive
Rules of inference: modus ponens, modus tollens, resolution; valid and invalid arguments
Predicates and quantifiers; nested quantifiers; negating quantified statements
Normal forms (CNF, DNF) and satisfiability; logic puzzles

syllabus.title: Proof techniques
topics: Axioms, definitions, theorems, lemmas; what a proof is and is not
Direct proof, proof by contrapositive, proof by contradiction, proof by cases
Existence and uniqueness proofs; counterexamples
Common errors: circular reasoning, proving the converse, division by zero
Proof that the square root of 2 is irrational; infinitude of primes

syllabus.title: Sets, functions and relations
topics: Set notation, subsets, power sets, Cartesian products; set operations and identities; Venn diagrams
Binary operations on sets; closure, associativity, commutativity, identity and inverse
Functions: domain, codomain, image; injective, surjective, bijective; composition and inverse
Relations: reflexive, symmetric, antisymmetric, transitive; equivalence relations and partitions
Partial orders, Hasse diagrams, lattices; closures of relations
Cardinality: countable and uncountable sets, Cantor's diagonal argument

syllabus.title: Number systems and number theory
topics: Integers, rationals, reals; positional number systems and base conversion
Divisibility, primes, the fundamental theorem of arithmetic
The division algorithm, Euclid's algorithm, extended Euclid and Bezout's identity
Modular arithmetic, congruences, inverses mod n; Fermat's little theorem and Euler's theorem
Chinese remainder theorem; RSA encryption as an application
Representing integers and floating-point numbers in a computer

syllabus.title: Sequences, series, induction and recursion
topics: Sequences and summation notation; arithmetic and geometric series; telescoping sums
Weak and strong induction; well-ordering principle; common induction mistakes
Recursive definitions of sequences, sets and functions; structural induction
Solving linear recurrences: characteristic equations, Fibonacci closed form
Recursive algorithms and proving them correct; towers of Hanoi, merge sort recurrence
Asymptotic notation: big-O, big-Omega, big-Theta

syllabus.title: Counting and combinatorics
topics: Sum and product rules; permutations and combinations; binomial theorem and Pascal's triangle
Pigeonhole principle and its generalisation
Inclusion-exclusion; derangements
Counting with repetition; stars and bars; distributing objects into boxes
Introduction to discrete probability: sample spaces, events, conditional probability

syllabus.title: Boolean algebra
topics: Boolean algebra as a mathematical structure; axioms and duality
Boolean functions, truth tables, sum-of-products and product-of-sums expressions
Simplification with identities and Karnaugh maps
Logic gates and circuits as Boolean expressions; functional completeness of NAND
Boolean algebra and set algebra as the same lattice

syllabus.title: Graph theory
topics: Graphs, digraphs, multigraphs; degree, handshaking lemma; adjacency matrix and list
Paths, cycles, connectivity, components; Euler circuits and Hamiltonian cycles
Trees, spanning trees, rooted trees; properties and counting of trees
Shortest paths with Dijkstra; minimum spanning trees with Kruskal and Prim
Graph colouring, chromatic number, bipartite graphs and matching
Planar graphs and Euler's formula; modelling road networks and timetables as graphs

courses.title: Fundamentals of Computer Science
topics: Overview of the computer
Information management
Files and databases
Computer networks, Internet and the Web
Technology and society
Computer safety and ethics
courses.description: A whole-degree tour of what a computer is, how information is represented and moved, and what computing does to society, so that every later course has a map to hang on. Taught to the depth of a leading introductory computer science survey, with hands-on exercises for every idea.
modelledOn: Brookshear and Brylow, Computer Science: An Overview
Schneider and Gersting, Invitation to Computer Science
Petzold, Code: The Hidden Language of Computer Hardware and Software
outcomes: Describe the parts of a computer and trace how a program and its data move from storage to processor and back.
Represent text, numbers, images and sound in binary and estimate storage and bandwidth needs.
Explain what algorithms, programs, operating systems and compilers are and how they fit together.
Organise information in files, spreadsheets and relational databases and query it.
Explain how the Internet and the Web work end to end, from a URL to a rendered page.
Reason about safety, privacy, ethics and the social impact of computing with Ghanaian and global examples.

syllabus.title: What computing is
topics: History of computing: from the abacus and Babbage to the transistor, the microprocessor and the smartphone
Computational thinking: decomposition, abstraction, patterns, algorithms
Hardware, software, data and people as the parts of a computing system
Kinds of computers: embedded, mobile, personal, server, supercomputer, cloud

syllabus.title: Representing information
topics: Bits and bytes; binary, hexadecimal; units from kilobyte to petabyte
Integers and two's complement; floating point and why 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3
Text: ASCII, Unicode and UTF-8; representing Twi and other Ghanaian languages
Images (pixels, colour depth, compression), sound (sampling, bit depth) and video
Compression: run-length, Huffman and the difference between lossless and lossy
Error detection: parity and checksums

syllabus.title: Inside the computer
topics: Logic gates and how they add; the processor, registers, clock and the fetch-decode-execute cycle
Memory hierarchy: registers, cache, RAM, SSD, hard disk, cloud storage
Input and output devices, buses and ports
Machine code, assembly, high-level languages, compilers and interpreters
Operating systems: what they do for programs and users; processes and files

syllabus.title: Algorithms and programs
topics: Algorithms as precise procedures; pseudocode and flowcharts
Sequence, selection and iteration; variables and data types
Searching and sorting by hand: linear search, binary search, bubble and selection sort
Why some algorithms are faster: counting steps, growth with input size
Writing and running short programs in Scratch and Python to see the ideas work
Software: system software, application software, open source, licences

syllabus.title: Information management, files and databases
topics: Data, information and knowledge; data quality and data life cycle
File systems, folders, file formats, metadata; backup and archiving
Spreadsheets for data: formulas, sorting, filtering, charts
Relational databases: tables, keys, relationships; simple SQL SELECT queries
Database applications: student records, mobile money ledgers, hospital systems
Big data and data centres: what changes at scale

syllabus.title: Computer networks, the Internet and the Web
topics: LANs, WANs, Wi-Fi, mobile data; switches and routers
IP addresses, DNS, packets and the layered model in plain terms
What happens when you type a URL: HTTP, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, servers and browsers
Email, cloud services, content delivery and why pages load slowly on poor links
Submarine cables and Ghana's connectivity; data costs and digital inclusion
Building a one-page website

syllabus.title: Computer safety, security and ethics
topics: Threats: malware, phishing, mobile money scams, social engineering
Passwords, two-factor authentication, encryption and HTTPS in plain terms
Personal data, privacy and Ghana's Data Protection Act
Professional ethics and the ACM Code; plagiarism and academic integrity
Safe and healthy computer use

syllabus.title: Technology and society
topics: Computing in Ghana and Africa: mobile money, agritech, e-government, health informatics
Automation, AI and the future of work; the digital divide
Environmental cost of computing: energy, e-waste at Agbogbloshie
Careers and the map of the computer science degree ahead

courses.title: Molecular Biology for Computing
topics: Cells and biomolecules
DNA structure and replication
Transcription and translation
Genes, genomes and mutation
Proteins and their functions
Laboratory techniques that produce data
Biological databases
courses.description: The molecular biology a computer scientist needs to work with biological data: cells and biomolecules, DNA structure and replication, transcription and translation, genes, genomes and mutation, protein structure and function, the laboratory techniques that generate sequence and expression data, and the databases that store it. Assumes no prior biology and is taught through interactive simulations of molecules and processes and small programs that manipulate real sequences in the browser, at the depth of a first-year molecular biology course for quantitative students.
modelledOn: Alberts et al., Essential Cell Biology
Watson et al., Molecular Biology of the Gene
Lodish et al., Molecular Cell Biology
Zvelebil and Baum, Understanding Bioinformatics
outcomes: Describe the structure of cells and the main classes of biomolecules and explain how their chemistry determines their function.
Explain DNA structure, replication and repair and represent sequences and their operations as strings and algorithms.
Trace the flow of information from gene to protein through transcription, RNA processing and translation, and implement it in code.
Classify mutations and genomic variation and predict their effects, using sickle cell disease and drug-resistant malaria as worked examples.
Relate protein structure to function and describe how enzymes, receptors and antibodies work.
Explain how sequencing, PCR, microarrays and other laboratory techniques produce data and retrieve and interpret records from biological databases.

syllabus.title: Cells and biomolecules
topics: Why computing needs biology: genomics, drug discovery, epidemiology and precision medicine
Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells; organelles; membranes and transport; viruses as a special case
Chemistry of life: water, bonds, pH; carbohydrates, lipids, nucleic acids and proteins
Energy and metabolism in outline: enzymes, ATP, respiration and photosynthesis
The cell cycle, mitosis and meiosis; how traits are inherited

syllabus.title: DNA structure and replication
topics: Nucleotides, the double helix, base pairing, antiparallel strands and 5' to 3' direction
Chromosomes, chromatin, histones and packaging; genome sizes across organisms
Semi-conservative replication: helicase, polymerases, primers, leading and lagging strands, Okazaki fragments
Replication errors, proofreading and DNA repair pathways
DNA as data: alphabets, reverse complements, GC content and k-mers written as small programs

syllabus.title: Transcription and translation
topics: The central dogma and its exceptions: reverse transcription in HIV, RNA viruses
Transcription: promoters, RNA polymerase, transcription factors, termination
RNA processing in eukaryotes: capping, polyadenylation, splicing and alternative splicing
The genetic code: codons, reading frames, start and stop codons, codon usage; translating sequences in code
Translation: ribosomes, tRNA, initiation, elongation, termination; post-translational modification
Gene regulation: operons, enhancers, epigenetics and non-coding RNAs in outline

syllabus.title: Genes, genomes and mutation
topics: Gene structure: exons, introns, untranslated regions, regulatory regions; genome organisation and repeats
Types of mutation: substitutions, insertions, deletions, frameshifts, copy number and structural variants
Sickle cell disease: the single substitution in the beta-globin gene, inheritance patterns and its prevalence in West Africa
Malaria and human genetics: the sickle cell trait, G6PD deficiency and balancing selection
Pathogen genomes: Plasmodium falciparum, drug-resistance mutations and genomic surveillance
Population genetics in brief: alleles, Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium, African genetic diversity

syllabus.title: Proteins and their functions
topics: Amino acids and their properties; peptide bonds
Levels of structure: primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary; folding and misfolding
Haemoglobin and how one amino acid change causes sickling
Enzymes and kinetics in outline; inhibitors and drug targets such as antimalarials
Antibodies, receptors and signalling; vaccines and the immune response
Predicting and visualising protein structure; the impact of structure prediction models

syllabus.title: Laboratory techniques that produce data
topics: Extraction, gel electrophoresis, restriction enzymes and cloning
PCR and quantitative PCR; rapid diagnostic tests for malaria and their limits
Sanger sequencing and next-generation sequencing: reads, quality scores, FASTQ files, coverage; long-read and portable sequencing
Measuring expression: microarrays and RNA-seq; mass spectrometry for proteins
Genome editing with CRISPR-Cas9 and its ethical questions
Sources of error and noise in experimental data; replicates and controls

syllabus.title: Biological databases
topics: Sequence formats: FASTA, GenBank and FASTQ; parsing them with code
Primary databases: GenBank, ENA and DDBJ; UniProt for proteins and the Protein Data Bank for structures
Genome browsers, Ensembl and variant databases such as dbSNP and ClinVar
Searching with BLAST and interpreting a result; ontologies such as the Gene Ontology
Data sharing, consent and benefit-sharing in African genomics research; capstone: annotate a malaria parasite gene from database records

courses.title: Principles of Programming
topics: Programming concepts and terminologies (LLL, HLL, translators)
Algorithms, pseudo-code, flowcharts
Character set, constants, data types, variables, operators, expressions
Flow control: if, if-else, switch, while, do-while, for
Basic object-oriented concepts
Identifying and fixing errors
courses.description: First contact with programming: thinking in algorithms, writing them as pseudocode and flowcharts, then as real code with variables, control flow, functions and a first look at objects. Taught to the depth of a leading first programming course, with a working program every week.
modelledOn: Zelle, Python Programming: An Introduction to Computer Science
Guttag, Introduction to Computation and Programming
Roberts, The Art and Science of Java
outcomes: Explain how source code becomes a running program and the roles of compilers, interpreters and linkers.
Design an algorithm for a stated problem and express it as pseudocode and a flowchart before coding.
Write programs that use variables, expressions, selection and loops correctly, and trace them by hand.
Decompose a program into functions with clear parameters and return values.
Explain objects, classes, attributes and methods and use simple objects in a program.
Find and fix syntax, runtime and logic errors with a systematic debugging method and tests.

syllabus.title: Programs, languages and translators
topics: What a program is; machine code, low-level and high-level languages; why there are many languages
Compilers, interpreters, assemblers and linkers; the edit-run-debug loop
Setting up an editor and running a first program; printing and reading input
Programming vocabulary: source, syntax, semantics, statement, expression, bug

syllabus.title: Algorithms, pseudocode and flowcharts
topics: Properties of an algorithm: finite, definite, effective; inputs and outputs
Pseudocode conventions; flowchart symbols for process, decision, loop, input/output
Tracing an algorithm with a trace table
Everyday algorithms: making change in cedis, computing a GPA, finding the largest of three numbers
From flowchart to code and back

syllabus.title: Data: character set, constants, types, variables
topics: Character set, identifiers, keywords and naming rules
Literals and constants; integer, floating-point, character, string and boolean types
Variables, declaration, assignment and memory as named boxes
Type conversion and casting; integer division and rounding surprises
Input, output and formatting numbers and strings

syllabus.title: Operators and expressions
topics: Arithmetic, relational, logical, assignment and increment operators
Precedence and associativity; evaluating expressions by hand
Boolean expressions and short-circuit evaluation
Common expression errors: off-by-one, mixing types, confusing = and ==

syllabus.title: Selection
topics: if, if-else, else-if ladders and nested ifs
switch statements and when to prefer them
Designing conditions: grade bands, tax brackets, leap years
Testing every branch; boundary values

syllabus.title: Iteration
topics: while, do-while and for loops; loop variable, condition, update
Counting, summing, averaging and finding maxima in a loop
Sentinel-controlled and flag-controlled loops; break and continue
Nested loops: multiplication tables, patterns, simple matrices
Infinite loops and termination; choosing the right loop

syllabus.title: Functions and program structure
topics: Defining and calling functions; parameters, arguments, return values
Scope and lifetime of variables; local and global
Decomposition and stepwise refinement; top-down design
Library functions: maths, strings, random numbers
Introduction to recursion: factorial and Fibonacci

syllabus.title: Collections and strings
topics: Arrays and lists: indexing, traversal, searching, finding min and max
Strings as sequences of characters; common string operations
Reading and writing a simple text file
Simple sorting by hand: bubble sort and selection sort

syllabus.title: Basic object-oriented concepts
topics: Objects as data plus behaviour; classes as blueprints
Attributes and methods; creating and using objects
Encapsulation and why it matters; a Student or BankAccount class
Objects already met: strings, lists, files

syllabus.title: Identifying and fixing errors
topics: Syntax, runtime and logic errors and how each shows itself
Reading error messages and stack traces
Debugging strategy: reproduce, isolate, hypothesise, test; print statements and a debugger
Writing test cases before and after fixing; defensive input checking
Code style, comments and documentation

courses.title: Spreadsheet Analytics
topics: Organising data in tables
Formulas, references and functions
Lookup and logical functions
Pivot tables and summaries
Charts in spreadsheets
What-if analysis and goal seek
Building a simple business model
courses.description: Using spreadsheets to organise, analyse and model data: structured tables, formulas and references, lookup and logical functions, pivot tables, charts, descriptive statistics, what-if analysis with goal seek and Solver, and building a sound business model. Every skill is practised on real-looking local datasets in a spreadsheet that runs in the browser, with each exercise checked automatically for correct formulas as well as correct answers.
modelledOn: Winston, Microsoft Excel Data Analysis and Business Modeling
Powell and Baker, Business Analytics: The Art of Modeling with Spreadsheets
Ragsdale, Spreadsheet Modeling and Decision Analysis
Microsoft Office Specialist: Excel Expert certification
outcomes: Organise raw data into clean, validated tables suitable for analysis.
Write correct formulas with relative, absolute and mixed references and use statistical, text, date, lookup and logical functions.
Summarise and explore data with conditional aggregation, pivot tables and descriptive statistics.
Choose and build charts and simple dashboards that communicate findings honestly.
Perform what-if analysis with data tables, scenarios, goal seek and Solver.
Build, document and check a small business model that separates inputs, calculations and outputs.

syllabus.title: Organising data in tables
topics: Rows as records and columns as fields; one table per subject; avoiding merged cells and blank rows
Data types and formats: numbers, text, dates, currency in cedis and percentages
Structured tables and named ranges
Data validation with drop-down lists and input rules
Sorting, filtering, removing duplicates, text to columns and importing CSV files
Running dataset: a market trader's daily sales log

syllabus.title: Formulas, references and functions
topics: Operators and precedence; relative, absolute and mixed references

Presenting results and recommendations to a non-technical owner

courses.title: Circuit Analysis
topics: Voltage, current, resistance and Ohm's law
Kirchhoff's laws, nodal and mesh analysis
Thevenin, Norton and superposition
Capacitors, inductors and transients
AC circuits, phasors and impedance
Power in AC circuits
Diodes and transistors as circuit elements
courses.description: Analysing linear electric circuits from Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws through nodal and mesh analysis, network theorems, first- and second-order transients, sinusoidal steady state with phasors and AC power, ending with diodes and transistors as circuit elements. Every circuit is built and measured on a simulated bench in the browser, with virtual meters and an oscilloscope checking each hand calculation.
modelledOn: Alexander and Sadiku, Fundamentals of Electric Circuits
Hayt, Kemmerly and Durbin, Engineering Circuit Analysis
Nilsson and Riedel, Electric Circuits
Sedra and Smith, Microelectronic Circuits (introductory chapters)
outcomes: Apply Ohm's law, Kirchhoff's laws and the passive sign convention to compute voltage, current, power and energy in resistive circuits.
Solve any linear circuit, including dependent sources and ideal op-amps, by nodal and mesh analysis in matrix form.
Simplify networks with superposition, source transformation and Thevenin and Norton equivalents, and design for maximum power transfer.
Derive and sketch the transient response of first- and second-order RC, RL and RLC circuits after switching.
Analyse circuits in sinusoidal steady state with phasors and impedance, and calculate real, reactive and complex power and power-factor correction.
Model diodes and transistors as circuit elements and design simple rectifier, regulator and switching circuits.

syllabus.title: Circuit variables and elements
topics: Charge, current, voltage, power and energy; the passive sign convention
Ideal independent and dependent (controlled) voltage and current sources
Resistance, Ohm's law, conductance and resistivity; open and short circuits
Power ratings and energy in kWh; reading a prepaid electricity meter and estimating a household bill
Measuring with ammeters, voltmeters and ohmmeters; meter loading errors

syllabus.title: Kirchhoff's laws and resistive circuits

Series and parallel resistors; voltage and current division

Equivalent resistance by inspection and by test source
Worked circuits: torch, charger and household lighting circuits

syllabus.title: Nodal and mesh analysis

Mesh-current method; supermeshes for current sources shared by meshes
Circuits with dependent sources; writing the equations in matrix form
Solving the systems by Gaussian elimination and Cramer's rule; checking with the simulator
Choosing between nodal and mesh analysis
The ideal operational amplifier as a circuit element: inverting, non-inverting, summing and difference amplifiers

syllabus.title: Network theorems
topics: Linearity and the superposition principle
Source transformation between voltage and current sources
Thevenin and Norton equivalents, including circuits with dependent sources
Maximum power transfer and its efficiency cost
Modelling a solar panel, battery and inverter as Thevenin sources for an off-grid home

syllabus.title: Capacitors, inductors and first-order transients

Source-free RC and RL circuits; the time constant
Step response of RC and RL circuits; initial and final values by inspection
Singularity functions: unit step, impulse and ramp
Switching transients and inrush current when power returns after a power cut
First-order op-amp circuits: integrator and differentiator

syllabus.title: Second-order circuits

Overdamped, critically damped and underdamped responses; damping ratio and natural frequency

Ringing and overshoot observed on the simulated oscilloscope

Impedance and admittance; series and parallel impedance combinations

syllabus.title: Power in AC circuits

Maximum average power transfer

Domestic wiring, earthing, fuses and circuit breakers; electrical safety

syllabus.title: Frequency response, resonance and coupled circuits

Passive low-pass, high-pass, band-pass and band-stop filters
Mutual inductance and the ideal transformer; step-down transformers in chargers and distribution

syllabus.title: Diodes and transistors as circuit elements

courses.description: Hands-on PC and laptop hardware: what every component does, how to choose, assemble, configure and repair a machine, and how to install and tune the operating system on it. Mueller, Upgrading and Repairing PCs
Andrews, Dark and West, CompTIA A+ Guide to IT Technical Support
outcomes: Identify every component on a motherboard and explain how CPU, chipset, memory and buses connect.
Choose and install processors, memory, storage, power supplies and expansion cards that are compatible with one another.
Configure BIOS/UEFI, boot order, secure boot and firmware updates safely.
Install and configure operating systems, drivers and printers on desktops and laptops.

courses.title: Game Design Principles
topics: What makes a game
Mechanics, dynamics and aesthetics
Level design
Balancing and difficulty
Narrative in games
Playtesting
Designing games for learning
courses.description: The craft of designing games that people want to play: what makes a game, the mechanics-dynamics-aesthetics framework, core loops, level design, balancing and difficulty, narrative, playtesting and designing games that teach. Every idea is prototyped first on paper and then in the browser, played on a phone by classmates and revised from what the playtests show.
modelledOn: Schell, The Art of Game Design: A Book of Lenses
Fullerton, Game Design Workshop: A Playcentric Approach to Creating Innovative Games
Salen and Zimmerman, Rules of Play: Game Design Fundamentals
Koster, A Theory of Fun for Game Design
outcomes: Define what makes a game and analyse existing games in terms of goals, rules, feedback and player choice.
Apply the mechanics, dynamics and aesthetics framework to design and critique a core gameplay loop.
Design levels that teach, pace and challenge players, using flow, difficulty curves and spatial layout.
Balance a game's economy, progression and difficulty using spreadsheets, simulation and playtest data.
Write game narrative that works with play, drawing on local stories such as Ananse tales and Ghanaian history.
Plan and run playtests, interpret the results and iterate a prototype into a finished game for learning or entertainment.

syllabus.title: What makes a game
topics: Definitions of play and games: goals, rules, conflict, outcome and voluntary participation; the magic circle
Formal elements: players, objectives, procedures, rules, resources, boundaries and outcomes
Types of fun and player motivation: Bartle's player types, self-determination theory, intrinsic and extrinsic reward
Traditional games as designed systems: oware, ludo, ampe and draughts analysed as rule sets
The designer's role and the iterative design cycle: idea, prototype, playtest, evaluate

syllabus.title: Mechanics, dynamics and aesthetics

Dynamics: feedback loops (positive and negative), rubber-banding, snowballing and player interaction
Aesthetics: the eight kinds of fun (sensation, fantasy, narrative, challenge, fellowship, discovery, expression, submission)
Meaningful choice, uncertainty and risk; the role of randomness and skill

syllabus.title: Core loops and prototyping

Paper prototyping with cards, dice and tokens; rapid digital prototyping in the browser
Game design documents, one-page designs and pitching a concept
Designing for constraints: touch input, small screens, intermittent data and low-end Android phones

syllabus.title: Level design

Procedural versus handcrafted levels; seeds, constraints and quality control
Puzzle design: clear rules, aha moments, hint systems and avoiding guesswork
Building and critiquing a level set for a small puzzle or platform game

syllabus.title: Balancing and difficulty
topics: Types of balance: symmetric and asymmetric, fairness, dominant strategies and transitive versus intransitive relations

Difficulty curves, dynamic difficulty adjustment and accessibility options
Progression systems: experience, unlocks, skill trees and avoiding grind

Iterating a prototype across two playtest rounds and reporting the changes

syllabus.title: Designing games for learning
topics: Serious games and gamification: what each is, and where points and badges help or hurt

Feedback, scaffolding and assessment inside the game; measuring whether learning happened
Case studies: games for literacy, mathematics, health and financial literacy (for example a susu savings game)
Designing for classrooms and community settings with shared or low-end devices

Guttag, Introduction to Computation and Programming Using Python

Process text, lists, dictionaries and files to solve information-processing tasks.
Choose and implement simple algorithms and reason about their running time.
Design classes with attributes, methods, inheritance and special methods.
Manipulate images and draw graphics programmatically.

while and for loops; range; break, continue, else on loops

courses.title: IT Support and Troubleshooting
topics: The role of IT support

Hardware faults
Operating system and software issues
Network connectivity problems

courses.description: The practical work of keeping people's computers and networks running: the role of IT support, a disciplined troubleshooting method, hardware faults, operating-system and software problems, network connectivity issues, managing users, accounts and printers, and the documentation and customer care that make support effective. Practised on simulated machines and networks in the browser where faults are injected and resolved, mirroring the realities of shared computers, internet cafes and frequent power cuts.
modelledOn: Meyers, CompTIA A+ Certification All-in-One Exam Guide
CompTIA A+ and Network+ objectives
ITIL service management foundation
outcomes: Describe the role of IT support and the service desk and how tickets flow and escalate.
Apply a structured troubleshooting method to isolate and resolve a fault.
Diagnose and remedy common hardware faults and power problems.
Resolve operating-system and application issues including boot, update and malware problems.
Diagnose network connectivity problems from the device to the internet.
Manage users, accounts and printers and document work with clear customer care.

syllabus.title: The role of IT support

syllabus.title: The troubleshooting method

syllabus.title: Hardware faults

syllabus.title: Documentation and customer care

courses.title: Linear Algebra for Data Science
topics: Vectors and vector spaces
Matrices and matrix operations
Systems of linear equations
Determinants and inverses
Eigenvalues and eigenvectors
Orthogonality and projections
Singular value decomposition and PCA
courses.description: The linear algebra that data science and machine learning run on: vectors and vector spaces, matrices and their operations, solving linear systems, determinants and inverses, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, orthogonality, projections and least squares, and the singular value decomposition behind principal component analysis. Each idea is seen geometrically in interactive browser plots, worked by hand, and then implemented in NumPy on real data.
modelledOn: Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra
Lay, Lay and McDonald, Linear Algebra and Its Applications
Boyd and Vandenberghe, Introduction to Applied Linear Algebra: Vectors, Matrices, and Least Squares
Deisenroth, Faisal and Ong, Mathematics for Machine Learning (linear algebra chapters)
outcomes: Represent data as vectors and matrices and reason about linear combinations, span, independence, basis and dimension.
Solve linear systems by Gaussian elimination and LU factorisation and interpret their solutions through the four fundamental subspaces.
Compute determinants and inverses and explain when a matrix is invertible and how conditioning affects numerical results.
Compute eigenvalues and eigenvectors, diagonalise matrices and apply them to dynamical systems and Markov chains.
Use orthogonality, projections, QR factorisation and least squares to fit models to data.
Derive and apply the singular value decomposition for low-rank approximation and principal component analysis.

syllabus.title: Vectors

Existence and uniqueness: consistent, inconsistent and underdetermined systems
LU factorisation and solving many right-hand sides; partial pivoting
Numerical issues: floating-point error, ill-conditioning and the condition number
Applications: balancing a mixing problem for animal feed and network flow

Diagonalisation, powers of a matrix and repeated linear maps

courses.title: Data Visualisation

courses.description: Turning data into charts and maps that people read correctly: how visual perception works, choosing the right chart for the question, colour, labelling and annotation, plotting with code, interactive web visualisation, geographic data and maps, and telling an honest story with data. Munzner, Visualization Analysis and Design
Wilke, Fundamentals of Data Visualization
Cairo, How Charts Lie: Getting Smarter about Visual Information

syllabus.title: Why visualise and the data behind a chart

Munzner's what, why and how framework: data abstraction, task abstraction and idioms
A short history: Playfair, Nightingale, Minard, Snow and Tukey

syllabus.title: Principles of visual perception

Gestalt principles: proximity, similarity, enclosure, connection, continuity and closure
Weber's law, area and angle judgement errors; why 3D and pie charts mislead
Change blindness, working memory limits and the data-ink ratio

syllabus.title: Choosing the right chart

Part-to-whole and hierarchy: stacked bars, treemaps, sunbursts and Sankey diagrams for flows
Small multiples and faceting; multivariate views and parallel coordinates
Matching a chart to a question about mobile money transaction volumes by region

syllabus.title: Colour, labels and annotation

Colour-vision deficiency, contrast ratios and accessible chart design
Titles that state the finding, direct labelling instead of legends, axis and tick choices
Annotation layers: highlighting, reference lines, callouts and uncertainty bands

syllabus.title: Plotting with code

syllabus.title: Interactive and web-based visualisation

syllabus.title: Data storytelling and avoiding misleading charts

courses.title: Digital Payments and Mobile Money
topics: Payment systems and clearing
Cards and online payments
Mobile money architecture
Agent networks
USSD and app channels
Interoperability between providers
Fraud and consumer protection
courses.description: How money moves electronically: payment systems, clearing and settlement, cards and online payments, the architecture of mobile money platforms, agent networks, USSD and app channels, interoperability between providers, and fraud and consumer protection, with Ghana's GhIPSS and mobile money market as the running case. Students design and simulate a working mobile money system in the browser, posting every transaction to a double-entry ledger and tracing it through the switch, the agent and the USSD menu.
modelledOn: CPMI-IOSCO, Principles for Financial Market Infrastructures
ISO 20022 and ISO 8583 financial messaging standards
PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard)
GSMA Mobile Money API specification and Mobile Money Certification
outcomes: Explain how payment systems clear and settle transactions and compare gross and net settlement and their risks.
Describe the card and online payment flows, their message standards and the security controls that protect them.
Design the architecture of a mobile money platform, including wallets, a double-entry ledger, the trust account and its APIs.
Analyse agent network operations, including float, liquidity and commissions, and USSD and app channel design.
Explain how interoperability between providers is achieved through a national switch and how disputes and reversals are handled.
Identify common payment fraud and evaluate controls, KYC tiers and consumer protection rules set by regulators.

syllabus.title: Money, payments and payment systems
topics: Functions of money; cash, central bank money, commercial bank money and e-money
Payment instruments: cash, cheques, credit transfers, direct debits, cards, mobile money and QR payments

syllabus.title: Payment systems and clearing

Cheque codeline clearing, ACH direct credits and debits, and instant payment systems such as GhIPSS Instant Pay
Settlement risk, liquidity risk and credit risk; collateral, prefunding and intraday liquidity

syllabus.title: Cards and online payments

PCI DSS requirements and reducing scope with hosted payment pages and tokens

syllabus.title: Mobile money architecture

syllabus.title: Agent networks

Descriptive, diagnostic, predictive and prescriptive analytics
BI architectures: data warehouse, data marts, data lake and lakehouse; Inmon versus Kimball
The BI tool landscape: open-source and commercial reporting, OLAP and dashboard tools

syllabus.title: Business questions and key performance indicators

Metrics versus KPIs; leading and lagging indicators; SMART targets
Balanced scorecard and strategy maps; KPI trees linking operations to goals
Defining a KPI precisely: formula, grain, filters, owner, target, frequency and data source
Perverse incentives and Goodhart's law
KPIs for a mobile money operator: active agents, float availability, transaction value and churn

syllabus.title: Dimensional models for reporting
topics: Kimball's four-step design: business process, grain, dimensions and facts
Star and snowflake schemas; transaction, periodic snapshot and accumulating snapshot fact tables
Additive, semi-additive and non-additive measures
Conformed dimensions and the bus matrix; the date dimension; degenerate and junk dimensions
Slowly changing dimensions types 1, 2 and 3; surrogate keys
Designing a sales star schema for a chain of pharmacies across Ghana's regions

syllabus.title: Extract, transform and load
topics: Source systems and extraction: full, incremental and change data capture

Transformations: lookups, surrogate key assignment, SCD handling and aggregation
ETL versus ELT; staging areas; orchestration and scheduling of pipelines
Testing pipelines: row counts, reconciliation, data quality rules and audit columns
Handling unreliable connectivity: batching uploads from branches and idempotent loads

syllabus.title: Querying and OLAP
topics: OLAP operations: slice, dice, drill-down, roll-up and pivot
Analytical SQL: GROUP BY with ROLLUP and CUBE, window functions, running totals and period-over-period comparisons
Cubes, aggregates and materialised views for performance
Semantic layers and calculated measures; time intelligence such as year to date

syllabus.title: Building dashboards
topics: Strategic, operational and analytical dashboards; designing for the audience and the decision
Layout and visual hierarchy; at-a-glance monitoring; bullet graphs and sparklines
Choosing charts for KPIs; showing targets, variance and trends; avoiding gauges and clutter
Filters, drill-through and interactivity; mobile layouts and low-bandwidth delivery
Usability testing a dashboard with real users; iterating on feedback
A district health dashboard of immunisation coverage and stock-outs

syllabus.title: Self-service analytics
topics: Self-service models: governed data sets, certified metrics and sandboxes
Designing a semantic model that business users can understand
Training and data literacy; the citizen analyst
Risks of self-service: conflicting numbers, spreadmarts and shadow IT

syllabus.title: Reporting for decision makers
topics: Structuring a management report: the answer first, evidence, and recommended action
Variance analysis and exception reporting; commentary that explains movements
Presenting uncertainty and data limitations honestly
Scheduled reports, alerts and distribution by email, SMS and messaging apps
Presenting findings on cocoa purchasing to a licensed buying company's board

syllabus.title: Data governance in organisations
topics: Data governance roles: owners, stewards and custodians; a data governance council
Data quality dimensions and measurement; master data and reference data management
Metadata, data catalogues, business glossaries and lineage
Security, row-level access and privacy; Ghana's Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843)
Capstone: an end-to-end BI solution with schema, pipeline, dashboard and governance plan

courses.title: Computer Graphics
topics: Raster and vector graphics
Line and circle drawing algorithms
2D and 3D transformations
Viewing and projection
Clipping and hidden surfaces
Shading and lighting
Introduction to WebGL
courses.description: From putting a pixel on the screen to rendering lit, shaded 3D scenes in the browser: rasterisation algorithms, transformations, viewing, clipping, visibility, shading and a working WebGL pipeline. Taught to the depth of a leading introductory computer graphics course.
modelledOn: Marschner and Shirley, Fundamentals of Computer Graphics
Hearn, Baker and Carithers, Computer Graphics with OpenGL
Cantor and Jones, WebGL Beginner's Guide
outcomes: Explain raster and vector representations, colour models and the graphics pipeline.
Implement line, circle and polygon rasterisation and filling algorithms and anti-aliasing.
Compose 2D and 3D transformations with homogeneous matrices and quaternions.
Set up cameras, projections and viewports and clip primitives against the view volume.
Resolve visibility with z-buffer and related methods and shade surfaces with Phong and physically based models.
Write WebGL programs with vertex and fragment shaders, buffers, textures and interaction.

syllabus.title: Raster and vector graphics
topics: Images as pixel grids; frame buffers, resolution, colour depth; displays from CRT to OLED
Colour: RGB, CMYK, HSV, gamma; colour perception and dithering
Vector graphics: paths, SVG, Bezier curves; scalable versus raster
The graphics pipeline overview: modelling, transformation, rasterisation, shading, display
Drawing pixels on an HTML canvas; image formats and compression (PNG, JPEG)

syllabus.title: Line, circle and polygon drawing algorithms
topics: DDA and Bresenham line algorithms; symmetry and integer arithmetic
Midpoint circle and ellipse algorithms
Scan-line polygon fill, edge tables, boundary and flood fill
Anti-aliasing: supersampling, Wu's algorithm, coverage
Thick lines, line styles and character rasterisation

syllabus.title: 2D transformations
topics: Translation, rotation, scaling, shear, reflection as matrices; homogeneous coordinates
Composition and order; rotation about an arbitrary point
Window-to-viewport mapping; coordinate systems
Hierarchical modelling: a 2D articulated figure

syllabus.title: 3D transformations and modelling
topics: 3D homogeneous transforms; rotation about arbitrary axes; Euler angles, gimbal lock, quaternions
Scene graphs and model-view hierarchies
Representing surfaces: polygon meshes, normals, indexed triangles; parametric surfaces and subdivision in brief
Loading and displaying an OBJ model

syllabus.title: Viewing and projection
topics: Camera model: eye, look-at, up; the view matrix
Orthographic and perspective projection matrices; field of view, near and far planes
Normalised device coordinates and the viewport transform
Depth precision and the perspective divide

syllabus.title: Clipping and hidden surfaces
topics: Cohen-Sutherland and Liang-Barsky line clipping; Sutherland-Hodgman polygon clipping; clipping in homogeneous space
Back-face culling
Z-buffer algorithm; painter's algorithm; BSP trees; scan-line visibility
Ray casting as an alternative; bounding volumes and spatial subdivision

syllabus.title: Shading and lighting
topics: Light sources: ambient, directional, point, spot; attenuation
Lambertian diffuse, Phong and Blinn-Phong specular; material properties
Flat, Gouraud and Phong shading; vertex normals
Texture mapping, mipmaps, bump and normal mapping; environment maps
Shadows (shadow maps), global illumination and ray tracing in brief; physically based rendering overview

syllabus.title: Introduction to WebGL
topics: WebGL context, buffers, attributes, uniforms; GLSL vertex and fragment shaders
Drawing triangles, applying matrices with a maths library, animation with requestAnimationFrame
Lighting and texturing in shaders; loading textures and models
Mouse and keyboard interaction: orbit camera, picking
Performance on low-end phones; three.js as a higher-level alternative
Project: an interactive 3D scene such as a model of a Ghanaian landmark or a data visualisation

courses.title: Computer Organization and Architecture
topics: Computer evolution and performance
Top-level view of function and interconnection
Cache memory
Instruction sets
Processor structure and function
RISC
Instruction-level parallelism and superscalar processors
Control unit operation
Microprogrammed control
Parallel processing
Multicore computers
Pipelining, memory hierarchy, virtual memory, I/O
courses.description: How a processor, its memory hierarchy and its I/O system are organised and why they perform as they do: instruction sets, datapaths, pipelining, caches, virtual memory, superscalar and multicore design, with a simulated processor built and measured along the way. Taught to the depth of a leading computer architecture course.
modelledOn: Stallings, Computer Organization and Architecture
Patterson and Hennessy, Computer Organization and Design
Hennessy and Patterson, Computer Architecture: A Quantitative Approach (selected chapters)
outcomes: Measure and reason about performance with execution time, CPI, Amdahl's law and benchmarks.
Describe an instruction set architecture and trace instructions through a single-cycle and a multi-cycle datapath.
Design a pipelined processor and handle structural, data and control hazards with forwarding, stalls and branch prediction.
Analyse cache and virtual memory behaviour and compute hit rates, miss penalties and address translations.
Explain hardwired and microprogrammed control and superscalar, out-of-order and multicore execution.
Describe I/O organisation, interrupts, DMA and the interconnection structure of a modern system.

syllabus.title: Computer evolution and performance
topics: Generations of computers; Moore's law, Dennard scaling and the end of frequency scaling
Performance metrics: execution time, throughput, clock rate, CPI, MIPS and their traps
Amdahl's law; benchmarks (SPEC) and performance comparison
Power, energy and cooling as design constraints; mobile versus server design points

syllabus.title: Top-level view of function and interconnection
topics: Von Neumann architecture; the instruction cycle with interrupts
Buses: address, data, control; arbitration, timing, hierarchies
Point-to-point interconnects: QPI, PCIe, on-chip networks
Program execution traced at the register-transfer level

syllabus.title: Instruction sets
topics: Machine instruction characteristics, operand types, data types, operations
Addressing modes and instruction formats; fixed versus variable length
RISC-V (or MIPS) as the running example: registers, loads and stores, arithmetic, branches, procedure calls, the stack
x86 and ARM compared; CISC versus RISC and the RISC argument
Translating C to assembly to machine code; the compiler, assembler, linker and loader
Floating point: IEEE 754 arithmetic in hardware

syllabus.title: Processor structure and function: the datapath
topics: Register organisation, user-visible and control registers, flags
Building a single-cycle datapath: instruction fetch, register file, ALU, data memory, control signals
Multi-cycle datapath and finite-state control
Control unit operation: micro-operations, hardwired control design
Microprogrammed control: control memory, microinstruction formats, sequencing, horizontal versus vertical
Implementing the datapath in a simulator and tracing a program

syllabus.title: Pipelining
topics: The five-stage pipeline; speedup and its limits; pipeline registers
Structural hazards; data hazards and forwarding; load-use stalls
Control hazards: stalling, delayed branches, static and dynamic branch prediction (BHT, BTB, two-bit predictors)
Exceptions and interrupts in a pipeline; precise exceptions
Deeper pipelines and their costs

syllabus.title: Instruction-level parallelism, superscalar and RISC
topics: RISC characteristics revisited: register windows, compiler scheduling, large register files
Superscalar execution: multiple issue, instruction window, dependencies (true, anti, output)
Out-of-order execution: register renaming, Tomasulo's algorithm, reorder buffer, speculation
VLIW and the limits of ILP; Spectre-style side channels as a consequence of speculation

syllabus.title: Cache memory and the memory hierarchy
topics: Locality and the memory hierarchy; SRAM versus DRAM; memory organisation and interleaving
Cache mapping: direct, set-associative, fully associative; block size, replacement policies, write policies
Multi-level caches; average memory access time; the three Cs of misses; cache-aware programming (matrix multiply)
Virtual memory: pages, page tables, TLBs, page faults; address translation worked examples; protection
Cache coherence in multiprocessors: snooping and MESI

syllabus.title: Input/output
topics: I/O modules, programmed I/O, interrupt-driven I/O, direct memory access
I/O channels and processors; buses and interfaces: USB, PCIe, SATA, NVMe
Storage: magnetic disks, SSDs, RAID levels; reliability and availability
Interrupt handling and the operating system's view of devices

syllabus.title: Parallel processing and multicore computers
topics: Flynn's taxonomy; SIMD and vector units; GPUs as throughput processors
Symmetric multiprocessors, NUMA, clusters; cache coherence and memory consistency
Multithreading: fine-grained, coarse-grained, simultaneous (hyper-threading)
Multicore organisation: shared caches, interconnects, heterogeneous cores (big.LITTLE in phones)
Parallel speed-up, Amdahl again, and writing a parallel program that scales

courses.title: Containers and Kubernetes
topics: Containers and images
Writing Dockerfiles
Container networking and storage
Kubernetes architecture
Pods, deployments and services
Configuration, secrets and scaling
Troubleshooting clusters
courses.description: Packaging and running software with containers and orchestrating it with Kubernetes: how containers isolate processes, building images with Dockerfiles, container networking and storage, the Kubernetes control plane, pods, deployments and services, configuration, secrets and autoscaling, and systematic troubleshooting of broken clusters. Practised hands-on in simulated terminals and a simulated multi-node cluster in the browser, taught to the depth of the Kubernetes administrator and developer certifications.
modelledOn: Burns, Beda, Hightower and Evenson, Kubernetes: Up and Running
Lukša, Kubernetes in Action
CNCF Certified Kubernetes Administrator (CKA) and Certified Kubernetes Application Developer (CKAD) curricula
Open Container Initiative image and runtime specifications
outcomes: Explain how containers use namespaces, control groups and layered file systems and contrast them with virtual machines.
Write efficient, secure Dockerfiles and multi-container applications and publish images to a registry.
Configure container networking and persistent storage for stateful and stateless workloads.
Describe the Kubernetes architecture and deploy applications with pods, deployments, services and ingress.
Manage configuration, secrets, resource limits and autoscaling and perform rolling updates and rollbacks.
Diagnose and repair failing workloads, nodes and cluster networking using a systematic troubleshooting method.

syllabus.title: Containers and images
topics: Why containers: dependency hell, environment drift, density; containers versus virtual machines
Linux foundations: namespaces, cgroups, capabilities, seccomp, union and overlay file systems
The OCI image format: layers, manifests, digests and tags; registries and pulling by digest
Container runtimes: Docker Engine, containerd, runc and Podman; rootless containers
The container life cycle: run, exec, logs, inspect, stop, remove; restart policies

syllabus.title: Writing Dockerfiles
topics: Dockerfile instructions: FROM, RUN, COPY, ENV, ARG, WORKDIR, USER, EXPOSE, ENTRYPOINT versus CMD
Layer caching and build order; .dockerignore; multi-stage builds for small images
Choosing base images: distroless, Alpine and slim images; image size on slow and metered connections
Image security: running as non-root, pinning versions, scanning for vulnerabilities, signing images
Containerising a Node.js API and a Python service; Docker Compose for multi-container development

syllabus.title: Container networking and storage
topics: Bridge, host and overlay networks; port publishing; DNS-based service discovery between containers
Network namespaces and virtual Ethernet pairs; inspecting traffic between containers
Volumes, bind mounts and tmpfs; data that must survive a container
Running a database in a container: persistence, backups and why it is often a bad idea in production

syllabus.title: Kubernetes architecture
topics: Why orchestration: scheduling, self-healing, scaling, rolling updates; the declarative model and reconciliation loops
Control plane: API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager, cloud controller manager
Worker nodes: kubelet, kube-proxy, the container runtime interface
Setting up a cluster with kubeadm; managed clusters on EKS, AKS and GKE; lightweight k3s for low-cost hardware
kubectl, kubeconfig, contexts and namespaces; reading and writing YAML manifests

syllabus.title: Pods, deployments and services
topics: Pods: multi-container patterns (sidecar, init containers, ambassador), pod life cycle, probes for liveness, readiness and startup
ReplicaSets and Deployments; rolling updates, rollout history and rollbacks
StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Jobs and CronJobs
Services: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer, headless services; endpoints and EndpointSlices
Ingress and the Gateway API; TLS termination; exposing a mobile money payment API through an ingress controller

syllabus.title: Configuration, secrets and scaling
topics: ConfigMaps and Secrets as environment variables and mounted files; encryption of secrets at rest; external secret stores
Resource requests and limits; quality of service classes; LimitRanges and ResourceQuotas
Scheduling: node selectors, affinity and anti-affinity, taints and tolerations, topology spread
Autoscaling: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, Vertical Pod Autoscaler, cluster autoscaler; metrics server
Persistent storage: PersistentVolumes, PersistentVolumeClaims, StorageClasses and dynamic provisioning
Packaging applications with Helm charts and Kustomize overlays

syllabus.title: Cluster security and networking
topics: Authentication and RBAC: service accounts, roles, role bindings, least privilege
Pod Security Standards and admission control; security contexts
The pod network model; CNI plugins such as Calico and Cilium; NetworkPolicies for isolation
Cluster DNS with CoreDNS; service meshes in brief

syllabus.title: Troubleshooting clusters
topics: A troubleshooting method: observe, hypothesise, test, fix, verify; reading events and describe output
Failing workloads: CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff, OOMKilled, pending pods and unschedulable nodes
Failing networking: services without endpoints, DNS failures, NetworkPolicy mistakes, ingress misrouting
Failing nodes and control plane: NotReady nodes, kubelet logs, certificate expiry, etcd backup and restore
Logging and monitoring a cluster with Prometheus, Grafana and centralised logs
Capstone: deploy, scale, secure and repair a multi-service application on a broken cluster under timed conditions

courses.title: Control Systems
topics: Modelling dynamic systems
Transfer functions and block diagrams
Time response and stability
Root locus
Frequency response: Bode and Nyquist
PID controller design and tuning
State-space models and digital control
courses.description: Analysis and design of feedback control systems: modelling physical systems, transfer functions and block diagrams, transient and steady-state response, stability, root locus, Bode and Nyquist methods, PID tuning, state-space design and digital control. Every plant and controller is simulated in the browser, so students tune a controller and immediately see its step response, root locus and frequency response move.
modelledOn: Nise, Control Systems Engineering
Ogata, Modern Control Engineering
Franklin, Powell and Emami-Naeini, Feedback Control of Dynamic Systems
Dorf and Bishop, Modern Control Systems
outcomes: Model electrical, mechanical and electromechanical systems as differential equations, transfer functions and state-space equations.
Reduce block diagrams and signal-flow graphs and determine transient response, steady-state error and stability.
Design compensators with the root locus and with Bode and Nyquist frequency-response methods to meet time- and frequency-domain specifications.
Design and tune PID controllers and explain integral windup, derivative filtering and practical tuning rules.
Design state-feedback controllers and observers, and implement controllers digitally with appropriate sampling.

syllabus.title: Introduction to feedback control
topics: Open-loop and closed-loop control; the benefits and costs of feedback
The control design process: specifications, model, design, simulation, implementation
Laplace transform review for control
Examples: water-tank level, room temperature, and a hydroelectric generator speed governor holding grid frequency at 50 Hz

syllabus.title: Modelling dynamic systems
topics: Electrical networks and operational amplifier circuits
Mechanical translational and rotational systems; gears and inertia reflection
Electromechanical systems: the armature-controlled DC motor
Thermal and fluid systems; electrical analogies
Linearisation of non-linear systems about an operating point
Identifying model parameters from measured step responses

syllabus.title: Transfer functions and block diagrams
topics: Transfer functions, poles and zeros; from differential equations to transfer functions
Block diagram algebra and reduction
Signal-flow graphs and Mason's gain formula
Effects of feedback: sensitivity to parameter variation, disturbance rejection, noise

syllabus.title: Time response, stability and steady-state error
topics: First-order response and the time constant
Second-order response: damping ratio, natural frequency, rise time, peak time, percentage overshoot, settling time
Higher-order systems and dominant poles; effect of zeros
Routh-Hurwitz stability criterion, including special cases
Steady-state error, system type and static error constants
Specifying performance for a solar-powered irrigation pump

syllabus.title: Root locus
topics: The root locus: angle and magnitude conditions
Sketching rules: asymptotes, breakaway and break-in points, imaginary-axis crossings, angles of departure
Gain selection to meet transient specifications
Lead, lag and lead-lag compensator design on the root locus
Root contours and parameter sensitivity

syllabus.title: Frequency response: Bode and Nyquist
topics: Frequency response and asymptotic Bode magnitude and phase plots
The Nyquist plot and the Nyquist stability criterion
Gain and phase margins; relation to transient response
Closed-loop frequency response and bandwidth; Nichols chart in brief
Lead, lag and lead-lag design in the frequency domain
Effect of time delay on stability, as in remote or networked control

syllabus.title: PID controller design and tuning
topics: Proportional, integral and derivative actions and their effect on response
Practical PID: integral windup and anti-windup, derivative filtering, set-point weighting, bumpless transfer
Tuning methods: Ziegler-Nichols, Cohen-Coon and IMC-based tuning
Cascade and feedforward control
Tuning a DC motor speed loop and a battery charge controller on the simulator

syllabus.title: State-space models
topics: State variables; converting between transfer functions and state-space forms
Solution of the state equation and the state-transition matrix
Controllability and observability
State feedback and pole placement; Ackermann's formula
Full-order observer design and the separation principle
The linear quadratic regulator in brief

syllabus.title: Digital control
topics: Sampled-data systems and the zero-order hold; z-domain transfer functions
Discretising controllers: forward, backward and Tustin approximations
Stability in the z-plane and the Jury test
Implementing a digital PID on a microcontroller: sampling-rate choice, quantisation and computational delay
Grid frequency control and load shedding as a large-scale control problem

courses.title: Digital Signal Processing
topics: Discrete-time signals and the DFT
The fast Fourier transform
FIR filter design
IIR filter design
Multirate processing
Spectral analysis
Audio and image processing applications
courses.description: Processing sampled signals with algorithms: the discrete Fourier transform and the FFT, FIR and IIR filter design and realisation, finite word-length effects, multirate systems, spectral estimation and applications to speech, audio and images. Each algorithm is implemented in code and run on real recordings in the browser, so every filter is designed, plotted, heard and measured against its specification.

Proakis and Manolakis, Digital Signal Processing: Principles, Algorithms and Applications
Lyons, Understanding Digital Signal Processing
Mitra, Digital Signal Processing: A Computer-Based Approach
